Case Vignette: "The Call He Couldn't Answer"

The patient is a 40-year-old married Middle Eastern man, a paramedic with 15 years of service. He presents for therapy at the urging of his wife, who has grown concerned about his increasing withdrawal, irritability, and sleeplessness over the past eight months. He is neat in appearance but holds his body rigidly, as if bracing for impact. His hands remain clasped in his lap, and he avoids eye contact when speaking of the event.

He begins by saying, "I've seen everything. Over a thousand calls. I thought I was immune." He describes his work with a quiet pride-the fast decisions, the dark humor shared with his partner, the satisfaction of stabilizing a patient in the field. He has always been able to compartmentalize, to leave the sirens at the station door. But eight months ago, that ability shattered.

The call came on a Tuesday afternoon, a clear day. He and his partner were dispatched to a multi-vehicle collision on the highway. As they approached, he recognized the make and color of a car-his younger brother's car. "I told myself it couldn't be. There are a thousand blue sedans in this city." But as he got closer, he saw the personalized license plate, a gift he had given his brother for his birthday.

His brother was trapped in the driver's seat, conscious, bleeding from a deep gash on his forehead. The patient's training took over-he assessed the scene, directed his partner, began stabilizing his brother's neck. But then his brother looked at him, eyes wide with fear and recognition, and said, "It hurts, big brother. It really hurts." The patient describes a physical sensation at that moment: "It was like the floor dropped out from under me. I was a paramedic for ten seconds. Then I was just a brother, and I could not breathe."

He performed his job. He cut his brother free, rode with him in the ambulance, held pressure on the wound. His brother survived, but with a traumatic brain injury that has left him with permanent cognitive deficits and a changed personality. He no longer recognizes the patient on bad days.

Since that day, the patient has not been the same. He continues to work, but he now volunteers for the least critical calls, avoiding any scene that involves a vehicle. He has started to check the dispatch notes before accepting a shift, scanning for any mention of a "motor vehicle collision." If he sees it, he calls in sick. He has used all his sick leave and is now on unpaid leave, but he tells himself he is "just resting."

At home, he is short with his wife and two children. He no longer plays with his youngest son, who is five, because the boy's laughter sounds too much like his brother's used to. He has stopped attending Friday dinners at his parents' house, making excuses about work. He feels a constant, low-grade dread, as if something terrible is always about to happen. He has begun to check his phone obsessively, waiting for a call that his brother has fallen or had a seizure.

He sleeps poorly, waking several times a night with a start, his heart pounding, convinced he hears sirens. He has vivid, intrusive images of his brother's face in the car, the smell of gasoline and blood. He tries to push these away by drinking two or three glasses of whiskey before bed, but it only makes him more groggy and irritable the next day.

He tells me, "I keep replaying it. What if I had been faster? What if I had called for a helicopter instead of driving? I was the one in charge. I should have saved him completely." He cannot accept that his brother survived. He feels that survival is not enough-that he failed to restore his brother to who he was. He is haunted by the idea that his brother's last clear memory is of pain and fear, and that he, the paramedic, did not take that away.

He has not told his colleagues about his brother. He is ashamed. He is supposed to be the one who stays calm. The one who fixes things. Now, he cannot even look at a car accident on television without his hands trembling. He sits in my office, a man who once ran toward chaos, now frozen by a single memory.
